summary: Summarizes the key features of OSPF version 2 and analyzes how the protocol will perform and scale in the Internet. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This report explains how OSPF version 2 shares network information and estimates the resources it needs. It concludes that router memory is the most likely limit as a network grows, while areas and stub areas can reduce some costs.

questions: what are the key features of ospf
how much memory does ospf need
what is the ospf designated router
subtitle: A review of OSPF version 2's features, resource costs and scaling limits.

tldr.problem: The IAB and IESG asked for an analysis of OSPF's features, resource use and limits before an Internet routing protocol advanced to Draft Standard status.
tldr.mechanism: The report describes OSPF version 2 and estimates its bandwidth, memory, CPU and Designated Router costs using measurements from three networks.
tldr.outcome: The report identifies router memory as the most likely limit on an OSPF system's size and notes that OSPF has limited ability to express policy.

today: RFC 1245 is an Informational report published in July 1991, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It analyzes OSPF version 2 as described in RFC 1247.

sections.title: Purpose of the Report
sections.content:
RFC 1245 reports on OSPF version 2, an Interior Gateway Protocol designed to route traffic inside one Autonomous System. The report was required as part of the process for an Internet routing protocol to advance to Draft Standard status.

It summarizes OSPF's main features and considers bandwidth, router memory, CPU use, and the load on a Designated Router. Its conclusions are based partly on statistics collected from three networks described in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: This report examines OSPF version 2, which helps routers choose paths inside one network administration. It estimates the resources the protocol uses and discusses where growth could cause limits.

sections.title: How OSPF Builds Routes
sections.content:
OSPF is a link-state routing protocol. Routers distribute link-state advertisements (LSAs), each describing part of the routing domain, and reliably flood changes so routers maintain the same link-state database. Each router uses that database to calculate a shortest-path tree rooted at itself.

OSPF also supports areas, external routes, virtual links, authentication of routing packets, equal-cost paths and variable-length subnet masks. A Designated Router has a special role on a multi-access network; a Backup Designated Router can take over if it fails.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF routers share descriptions of network links and keep matching copies of that information. Each router uses its copy to calculate the best paths from its own location.

sections.title: Bandwidth, Memory and CPU Costs
sections.content:
The report estimates that an AS external LSA is 36 bytes and that about three LSAs fit in a packet. In the measured networks, advertisements were refreshed on average close to every 30 minutes. With a 5% link-bandwidth allowance, its calculation gives 2,087 external advertisements for a 9.6 Kb link and 12,174 for a 56 Kb link.

For memory, the report estimates 64 bytes per external LSA including support data, or 640K bytes for 10,000 such LSAs. It says Dijkstra calculations were infrequent in the measured networks, while dividing a routing domain into areas can limit the calculation to one area at a time.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF sends its route information infrequently, which limits the bandwidth it uses. The report says memory is a more likely constraint because routers must store the routing information.

sections.title: Designated Router Load and System Limits
sections.content:
All routers on a network send Hello packets, generally every 10 seconds. The Designated Router handles more link-state updates and acknowledgments than other routers, so it could encounter a traffic limit first. The report cites simulations with more than 50 routers on one LAN and interoperability tests with 13 routers on one Ethernet without problems.

The report considers router memory the most likely limit to the size of an OSPF system. It also identifies slow links, costly shortest-path calculations and too many routers on one network as possible constraints. Default routes and stub areas are among the ways it describes to reduce routing information.
sections.plainLanguage: The Designated Router carries more routing messages than other routers on the same network. The report expects memory to limit overall network size before that message load becomes a problem.

sections.title: Suitable Networks and Policy Limits
sections.content:
The report considers OSPF suitable for both large and small Autonomous Systems. It highlights transit systems because OSPF can import many external routes and update an individual external route without recalculating every route. It also identifies features useful to smaller standalone or stub systems.

OSPF has limited ability to express policy: its main policy mechanism is a four-level routing hierarchy. The report says a system that needs more sophisticated policy would need separate Autonomous Systems connected by a policy-based Exterior Gateway Protocol. The RFC states that it does not discuss security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The report sees OSPF as useful in both large and small networks. It also says OSPF alone cannot express complex routing policies.

references.text: Moy, J., "Experience with the OSPF protocol", RFC 1246, July 1991.
